summary: Some of the guards report the empty tomb to the chief priests, who pay them a large sum to say the disciples stole Jesus’ body while they slept.
key_insight: The chief priests did not claim the body was still in the tomb. Their story admitted the tomb was empty and argued only about how it became empty. And the guards were told to vouch for what happened while they were asleep.
story: While the women were on their way to the disciples, some of the guard came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened at the tomb.

The chief priests gathered with the elders and consulted together. Then they gave the soldiers a large sum of money with a story to tell: “Tell them, ‘His disciples came at night and stole Him away while we slept.’” They added a promise: “And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will appease him and make you secure.”
So the soldiers took the money and did as they were instructed. Matthew adds that this saying “is commonly reported among the Jews until this day.”

scene.label: Whose guard?
scene.text: When the priests asked for a guard, Pilate answered, “You have a guard” (27:65). Pilate may have been granting them Roman soldiers, or telling them to use their own temple police. The worry about the governor and the promise to keep the men safe fit Roman soldiers best, though interpreters differ.

scene.label: Asleep on watch
scene.text: A Roman soldier who slept at his post could be severely punished, even put to death. Confessing to it was a real risk, which is why the soldiers needed both a large payment and a promise of protection.

scene.label: The council meets
scene.text: The chief priests and elders were leading members of the Sanhedrin, the council that had condemned Jesus only days before. They answered the guards’ report with a meeting, a payment and a cover story.

scene.label: “Until this day”
scene.text: Matthew wrote some decades later, and the stolen-body story was still being told. In the middle of the second century, Justin Martyr, in his dialogue with a Jew named Trypho, said the same charge was still being spread.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew alone tells of the guard, from the sealing of the tomb (27:62–66) to this report. His words “until this day” show that his readers were still hearing the stolen-body story, and he answers it by telling what happened: the leaders asked for the guard, and then paid for the lie. Money marks the chief priests in Matthew, from Judas’s thirty pieces of silver (26:15) to this “large sum.”

seeing.reveals: Even the enemies of Jesus bore witness to the empty tomb. The resurrection was not a rumor His friends invented; it was news His enemies paid to cover up.
seeing.living: The guards had felt the earthquake and seen the angel, and still they took the money. Evidence alone does not change a heart that has reasons not to believe. Ask honestly what it would cost you to live as though Jesus is alive, and do not let that cost decide what you believe about Him.
seeing.ponder: What “large sum” of comfort, approval or security might tempt you to keep quiet about the risen Jesus?

preaching.big_idea: Money can buy a story, but it cannot fill an empty tomb.
preaching.watch_for: Read 27:62–66 alongside this passage. The leaders remembered Jesus’ words, “After three days I will rise,” better than His disciples did, and the guard they posted to stop a resurrection story became witnesses of the empty tomb.
